newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end narrowly mixed as data awaited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end narrowly mixed as data awaited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended the week narrowly mixed Friday, stuck in a hard place and facing a rock in the form of next week's nonfarms payrolls report.
The strength of job growth in February will obviously determine whether the market can bounce off the employment report without sinking further. The mood this session was decidedly pessimistic again.
The Treasury's 30-year bond ended unchanged at 97-23/32 to yield 6.80 percent. Trading volume remained heavy early on, but fell off during the afetrnoon.

Traders said the data seen on Friday had little lasting impact, with the market still feeling a strong negative bias after Federal Reserve Board chief Alan Greenspan warned on Wednesday that the Fed might tighten without strong inflation numbers and added that soaring stock prices could be based on overexuberance.

"The numbers had little if any effect on the market today as we stayed pretty much in the 1/4- to 3/4-point most of the day. The statistics today confirmed the notion that the economy remained on a solid footing," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

"Next week the story will be Greenspan and the employment report, although Greenspan probably won't have anything to say that's toughening nor softening," Flanagan said. Greenspan was scheduled to deliver the delayed second leg of his Humphrey Hawkins testimony to the House Wednesday.
"He just wanted to give a shot across the financial markets' bow and he did that Wednesday," Flanagan said.

He said that in addition to the overall number there would be particular interest in two nuances of the report -- wages, and the security workers feel to quit jobs and find others -- Greenspan has ssaid he will pay close attention to.

The worker security portion is contained in the "job leavers" category of the household survey which jumped from 7.97 percent last October to 8.90 percent in January -- about a 12 percent hike, Flanagan said.
"By then Greenspan will have spoken twice and if conditions warrant he'll be forced to move," Flanagan said. Equities will not be the catalyst even if the DJIA should shoot up 500 points, he said.
Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp., agreed that Friday's numbers had little effect on trading volume or price levels.
Friday's economic data simply paled in importance in front of the National Association of Purchasing Management survey on Monday and the employment report on Friday, Schaja said.

The first three reports of Friday's trading session drew little reaction. The first revision of fourth-quarter GDP was downward to 3.9 percent from 4.7 percent. The University of Michigan's final February reading was said higher.
An overall higher Chicago purchasing report lent some brief support on weaker employment and prices paid components.
DLJ's Schaja said there would be three key components to Monday's NAPM report -- prices, employment and deliveries.
Three-month bill rates rose three basis points to 5.10 percent. Six-month bill rates were three basis points higher at 5.17 percent and year-bill rates were one basis point higher 5.36 percent.

Two-year notes ended down 2/32 at 99-19/32, yielding 6.09 percent. Five-year notes closed at 99-13/32, down 2/32, yielding 6.39 percent. Ten-year notes ended at 97-25/32, unchanged to yield 6.56 percent.
